title: Giving Measurements a Place
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Three thermometers give us three readings. Before we can calculate with them, we need to decide how those readings are stored, which position belongs to which thermometer, and what an operation should do to the collection.

title: Which Direction Are We Adding?
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: A table can hold several greenhouses across several days. Adding across a row answers a different question from adding down a column. We need to keep that distinction when we ask an array to calculate.

title: Preparing the Arrays We Need
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Botie needs a place for tomorrow's readings and a set of times at which to collect them. We can describe those arrangements directly instead of typing every repeated value ourselves.

title: Choose the Readings Without Losing Their Place
blurb: Botie may need one morning, a run of mornings, or selected greenhouses. We need to express each request precisely and know whether editing the selection will change the original report.

title: Put the Same Readings Into the Right Arrangement
blurb: A sensor may send one long sequence while a calculation expects rows. We need to change the arrangement without changing which measurements belong to each day and greenhouse.

title: One Reference for Many Rows
blurb: Each greenhouse has its own target temperature. We want to compare every day's readings with those three targets without copying the targets into a new table by hand.

title: Ask Each Row a Question
blurb: Botie needs the greenhouse readings that reached a temperature limit. A yes-or-no decision for each reading lets us select the relevant observations without losing their order.

title: Summarise a Report Without Losing the Question
blurb: Botie needs totals, typical readings, and the greenhouse that needs attention first. A value, a position, and an ordered report answer different questions, even when they come from the same array.

title: One Calculation for a Whole Report
blurb: Botie applies the same rule to many readings. We will first write the repeated steps, then express them with array operations while keeping the intermediate values and memory costs understandable.

title: Turn Several Measurements Into Several Predictions
blurb: A prediction can combine temperature and humidity with separate coefficients. Matrix operations let us apply that same rule to every greenhouse, then check how a fitted rule relates to its observations.

title: When Two Calculations Almost Agree
blurb: A tiny rounding difference, a missing observation, and a wrongly shaped result are different problems. We need checks that distinguish them before trusting a numerical answer.

title: Can We Repeat the Same Experiment?
blurb: Changing both a model and its sampled observations makes it difficult to explain a changed result. We need to keep track of the random choices so we can repeat a comparison.

title: Give a Reusable Calculation a Clear Contract
blurb: Copying a calculation into every exercise makes mistakes hard to repair. We will put the rule in a function, state what its inputs mean, and check it on more than one report.

title: Keep Enough of a Calculation to Run It Again
blurb: A printed table is not a complete experiment record. We will save arrays with their shapes and types, keep related arrays together, and check what survives when a report moves through a text file.

title: What Does One Row Actually Describe?
blurb: Botie has an asset list and a stack of inspection notes. Decide what belongs on each row before asking the database a question.

title: Which Columns Answer the Question?
blurb: A report needs the kinds of equipment at each site. Choose the relevant fields and decide exactly which repeated rows should disappear.

title: Which Inspection Records Need Our Attention?
blurb: Translate a maintenance question into conditions on individual rows, and make the grouping of those conditions explicit.

title: Which Two Visits Took the Longest?
blurb: Build a reproducible top list, including what happens when two records have the same value.

title: Was the Visit Instant, or Is Its Duration Missing?
blurb: Keep an unknown measurement distinct from zero, and follow SQL’s true, false and unknown conditions.

title: What Should Botie Label Each Reading?
blurb: Express a row-level decision with CASE while keeping unknown measurements visible and using fallbacks deliberately.

title: How Much Inspection Time Did We Actually Record?
blurb: Turn visit rows into a summary without confusing the number of visits with the number of known durations.

title: How Much Work Belongs to Each Asset?
blurb: Form a separate group for each asset, then calculate summaries without mixing visits from different equipment.

title: Which Assets Keep Returning with the Same Finding?
blurb: Filter individual inspections before grouping, then filter the groups according to the evidence they contain.

title: Which Site Does Each Inspection Belong To?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Connect inspection facts to the asset register by a declared key, then inspect the row pairs the join actually produces.

title: Which Assets Have No Matching Inspection?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Keep the whole asset register while attaching whatever qualifying inspection evidence exists.

title: Why Did Joining Readings Double the Inspection Total?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Trace a many-to-many multiplication, then summarise each event stream at the intended grain before combining it.

title: Which Inspections Took Longer Than the Usual Visit?
blurb: Use one query’s result inside another without losing track of whether that result is one value, several rows, or a value belonging to the current asset.

title: Which Pumps Still Have No Completed Visit?
blurb: Ask whether a related row exists, keep the outer row’s identity, and avoid treating an unknown key as evidence that every candidate is present.

title: Which Pumps Appear on Either List but Are Still Unfinished?
blurb: Combine, compare and subtract query results while keeping duplicate policy, column meaning and final ordering explicit.

title: Can We Read the Query in the Order We Explain the Job?
blurb: Use common table expressions to name meaningful query stages while keeping grain, scope and execution assumptions explicit.

title: How Far Does the Failed Supply Line Reach?
blurb: Follow a hierarchy or dependency graph using an anchor, a repeated join and explicit safeguards against cycles and excessive traversal.

title: Keep Every Reading While Looking at Its Neighbours
blurb: Partition and order individual records for row numbers, ranks and previous-reading comparisons without collapsing them into groups.

title: Which Readings Belong in This Rolling Total?
blurb: Choose ROWS, peer groups and time ranges deliberately so rolling calculations include the observations the question actually describes.

title: Where Did the Quiet Day Go?
blurb: Define UTC timestamps, half-open reporting intervals and a calendar spine so missing days do not disappear or midnight events get counted twice.

title: Why Did a Pump Search Return the Wrong Equipment?
blurb: Clean and compare text under an explicit identifier policy, with literal pattern characters, NULL handling and honest Unicode limits.

title: Is That Temperature a Number or Just Text?
blurb: Extract structured payloads with explicit JSON validity and type checks while preserving the distinction between missing, null, text and numeric data.

title: What Could the Model Have Known at That Moment?
blurb: Build one feature row per historical decision using event time, availability time and explicit label boundaries, without leaking later evidence into the inputs.

title: What Does One Equipment Record Promise?
blurb: A column called cost can hold cents, pounds or an unexplained string. Give the maintenance team a table whose identities and units mean the same thing on every row.

title: Can a Job Refer to a Pump We Have Never Recorded?
blurb: A row can have the right types and still contain an impossible reference. Put identity, domain and relationship rules at the database boundary.

title: Why Must a Pump Move Be Edited on Every Job?
blurb: Repeated asset details make updates disagree. Find which identity determines each fact and give that fact one deliberate home.

title: Change the Requested Jobs Without Rewriting the Rest
blurb: New inspections arrive, existing ones change, and cancelled drafts leave the queue. Give each write a precise target and preserve newer information.

title: Move Spare Parts Without Losing Half the Transfer
blurb: A transfer changes two stock balances and its audit record. Make those changes one unit of work, and learn what a rollback can actually undo.

title: What If Someone Changes the Job While Botie Is Reading It?
blurb: Two valid edits can overwrite each other. Make stale assumptions visible, and distinguish version checks from the database’s isolation guarantees.

title: Find One Pump’s Readings Without Checking Every Pump
blurb: The reading table keeps growing. Arrange useful lookup keys so the database can find a small candidate region, then account for the cost of maintaining that structure.

title: Why Does a Short Query Repeat So Much Work?
blurb: A compact query can scan the same table repeatedly. Read the access plan, preserve the answer, and compare work on data that resembles the real job.

title: Let a Search Value Stay a Value
blurb: A search box should select an asset, not rewrite the query or change whose records are visible. Keep values, query structure and permissions at separate boundaries.

title: Which Sensor Records Should Reach the Training Table?
blurb: A query can run successfully over duplicate identities, missing readings and impossible timestamps. Turn the dataset’s assumptions into visible checks before building model features.

title: Pick Up New Changes Without Losing Late Readings
blurb: Repeated full imports become expensive, but a naive timestamp filter misses corrections and deletions. Track source change position, merge versions and commit the checkpoint with the result.

title: Which Records Does the Technician Need Together?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A pump screen, a recent-reading lookup and a site report ask different questions of the same records. Start with those requests before choosing how to store the data.

title: Which P1 Did the Lookup Mean?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: Two sites use the same short asset ID. Build keys that preserve the full identity, and distinguish a missing entry from a stored zero.

title: How Long Should Botie Trust the Saved Reading?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A cache can answer quickly while showing an old reading. Follow its expiry boundary and the load a cold cache sends back to the source.

title: Can One Record Describe the Pump and Its Sensor?
blurb: Read a nested maintenance record field by field. Keep missing data separate from null, preserve measurement types, and decide which rules every document must follow.

title: Should Every Pump Keep a Copy of the Supplier’s Phone Number?
blurb: A copied contact becomes stale when the supplier changes its number. Separate facts owned by a pump from shared current facts and intentional historical snapshots.

title: Did the High Value Belong to the Temperature Sensor?
blurb: An array contains several readings. Keep the sensor kind and its value attached to the same member while filtering documents.

title: Can Botie Save a Change Without Erasing Somebody Else’s?
blurb: A technician saves an old copy after another editor has changed the pump. Keep unrelated fields intact and bind the write to the version that was actually reviewed.

title: Can We Find North’s Hot Pumps Without Reading Every Document?
blurb: Use a site index to narrow the candidates, then keep the temperature condition. Inspect what an index saves and which work it leaves behind.

title: How Much Urgent Work Was Hidden Inside the Pump Documents?
blurb: Follow documents through filtering, array expansion and grouping. Keep track of what one row represents so the site total counts visits exactly once.

title: Why Is One Storage Key Doing All the Work?
topic: Partitioning for the Questions We Ask
blurb: The maintenance service has plenty of records but most requests land on one tenant. Choose a key from the work the service actually performs, then inspect the traffic it concentrates.

title: Keep One Asset’s History Together Without Growing Forever
topic: Partitioning for the Questions We Ask
blurb: A technician wants a time range for one pump. Give that request a bounded partition and an ordering that makes the required records reachable.

title: Why Did the Repair Disappear When Botie Read It Back?
blurb: Copies can disagree while an update is travelling. Define what a particular read must guarantee before deciding which replica may answer it.

title: Two Technicians Cannot Both Reserve the Last Kit
blurb: A successful read does not reserve the stock it showed. Put the expected version and remaining-stock rule inside the actual write.

title: How Can Two Offline Teams Keep Both Inspection Counts?
blurb: Choosing the last arriving total can lose someone’s work. Give each replica an owned contribution and derive a merge whose repeated delivery does not inflate the count.

title: Why Does the Dashboard Still Count a Job That Was Closed?
blurb: A source record changes while a dashboard keeps its own count. Build a projection from versioned job images and make repeats, moves and deletions visible.

title: The New Sensor Sends a Different Document
blurb: Some readers still expect temp_c while a new device sends a value and a unit. Introduce an explicit representation version and a reader that can explain both.

title: The Bad Update Reached Every Replica. What Can We Restore?
blurb: Replication faithfully copies a mistake too. Recover a known snapshot through a complete log interval, then verify the recovered service before switching readers.

title: A Fast Feature Lookup Still Has to Mean the Right Thing
blurb: A model needs the right entity, feature definition and available measurements in a fixed order. Use a serving document for that contract while keeping historical training evidence separately.

title: Which Equipment Depends on This Supply?
blurb: Represent equipment and its directed dependencies as nodes and relationships before choosing how to query the connections.

title: Are These Two Pumps Actually the Same Pump?
blurb: Separate durable identity from names, qualify external IDs by their source and detect collisions before merging records.

title: Who Inspected This Pump?
blurb: Match a connected pattern and preserve variable bindings across steps instead of accidentally combining unrelated records.

title: How Many Inspections Were Actually Completed?
blurb: Filter bound properties and aggregate at the intended grain, distinguishing paths, relationships and distinct inspection identities.

title: Keep the Pumps That Have No Completed Inspection
blurb: Use optional graph patterns without losing the starting population or mistaking an unmatched placeholder for a real inspection.

title: Follow a Dependency Without Following It Forever
blurb: Separate reachability from path enumeration, handle cycles explicitly and interpret bounded traversal results without promising complete discovery.

title: The Route with Fewer Stops Takes Longer
blurb: Distinguish minimum-hop paths from minimum-cost paths and implement Dijkstra’s nonnegative-cost frontier with explicit unreachable and tie semantics.

title: Which Rules Must Every Asset Write Preserve?
blurb: Separate key presence, uniqueness and lookup performance, then audit existing data before installing graph constraints.

title: The Graph Changed While the Approval Was Waiting
blurb: Treat approvals and snapshot checks as preparation, then use authorised, parameterised transactions with explicit conflict and retry behaviour.

title: A Replayed Import Must Not Create Another Relationship
blurb: Stage graph imports by stable identity, distinguish exact replays from conflicts and preserve rejected records instead of silently losing relationships.

title: Why Did One More Hop Make the Query So Expensive?
blurb: Read query plans, reason about candidate expansion and compare access paths without confusing a toy operation count with measured database performance.

title: Can Two Teams Describe the Same Resource?
blurb: Distinguish resource identifiers from literals, read RDF statements and build SPARQL patterns without confusing RDF with the property-graph model.

title: Where Did This Maintenance Claim Come From?
blurb: Represent claims and their sources, retain contradictions and apply explicit time boundaries before using graph evidence.

title: Which Connected Records Can the Assistant Use?
blurb: Build bounded graph retrieval with access and time boundaries, then preserve evidence and measure whether the added context actually helps.

title: What Does One Row Represent?
blurb: Two identical-looking rows might be a duplicated import or two genuine observations. We need to establish a record's identity before cleaning a dataset or trusting its counts.

title: When a Measurement Is Missing
blurb: An empty thermometer reading does not mean the greenhouse was at zero degrees. We need to distinguish what was measured from what we supplied to keep a calculation working.

title: Categories Without an Invented Ranking
blurb: A roof can be glass, plastic, or mesh. Assigning those names arbitrary numbers can accidentally suggest a ranking. We need a representation that preserves category membership without inventing a numerical relationship.

title: When the End Is Beside the Beginning
blurb: The hour after 23 is zero, yet ordinary subtraction puts those hour numbers far apart. A repeating feature needs a representation that keeps its beginning beside its end.

title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: A model can appear remarkably accurate when a feature contains information that arrives after the decision. We need to reconstruct what was actually available when each prediction would have been made.

title: When the Important Class Is Rare
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: If almost every sensor is healthy, predicting healthy every time can look accurate while missing every failure. We need to inspect what the score says about each class.

title: What Must a Model Improve On?
blurb: A complicated predictor needs a simple comparison. Before fitting one, we can measure how well a rule that always predicts a training average performs on new observations.

title: Would More Examples Help?
blurb: Before collecting more data or choosing a more flexible model, we can examine how training and validation errors change as the training set grows.

title: When Should a Probability Become an Action?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A probability is evidence, not a complete instruction. We need to decide how likely a sensor failure must be before an inspection is worth its cost.

title: Does Eighty Percent Mean Eighty Percent?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A model can rank failures well and still overstate its probabilities. We need to compare its confidence with what actually happens across similar predictions.

title: Have We Really Held Out a New Example?
blurb: Several rows can belong to the same greenhouse, patient, or device. If we want to predict for a new entity, a random row split can put familiar entities on both sides of the evaluation.

title: What Changed After the Model Was Fitted?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: A model tested on one mix of conditions may later face another. Comparing the incoming data with the reference data helps us notice changes without pretending that every change proves an accuracy failure.

title: How Much Does Our Estimate Depend on This Sample?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: One average hides how it might change if different observations had been collected. Resampling the observed data gives us a way to study that dependence under explicit assumptions.

title: What Are the Errors Trying to Tell Us?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: The temperature errors average to zero, but the greenhouse is still too hot some mornings. Keep each mistake beside the reading that produced it and work out what the average concealed.

title: Which Alerts Deserve an Inspection?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: A fault detector can look accurate while missing almost every fault. Follow the alerts and the faults separately, then choose a threshold the inspection team can actually use.

title: Better for Which Cases?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: Most readings come from the day shift. A model can improve its overall score while getting worse at night. Keep group sizes beside group errors before calling that a repair.

title: Did the Revision Help on the Same Cases?
blurb: A lower score on an easier dataset tells us little about a revision. Match the cases, inspect their gains and regressions, then resample the paired observations to explore uncertainty.

title: Who Checks the Model-Choosing Process?
blurb: Trying enough settings can produce an attractive validation score by chance. Put the search inside a separate assessment so the result includes the cost of choosing.

title: Is the Model Wrong, or Is the Record Wrong?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: A suspicious label deserves a closer look. Use out-of-fold disagreements to organise review while preserving original records and the boundary around the final assessment.

title: When Should the Model Ask for Help?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: Sending uncertain cases to a person changes both the error rate and the workload. Measure what the model handles and what it leaves for the review team.

title: Should This Change the Prediction?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: The same measurement can arrive in different units or a different batch. State the behaviour that should survive those changes, then test the actual prediction pipeline.

title: Repair the Night-Shift Model Without Breaking the Day Shift
topic: Build and Check a Model Revision
blurb: Diagnose a missing condition, fit a revised predictor and compare it with the baseline. Botie then checks whether the overall gain survives group and runtime requirements on a fresh shift.

title: What Does an Alarm Tell Us?
blurb: An alarm may catch most faulty sensors and still be wrong surprisingly often. We need to know how common faults are before deciding what an alarm means.

title: Which Rule Could Have Produced These Observations?
blurb: A probability rule predicts possible observations. Likelihood holds the observations fixed and compares the rules that might have produced them. That distinction connects probability to fitting a model.

title: Naive Bayes
blurb: A warm casing and an unstable reading may each suggest a faulty sensor. We need a way to combine those clues, while being explicit about what we assume about their relationship.

title: Support Vector Machines and Margins
blurb: Several lines may separate the same labelled examples. We need a reason to prefer one, and a way to handle examples that cannot all be separated cleanly.

title: Hierarchical Clustering
blurb: A collection can have small groups inside larger groups. Joining the closest groups one step at a time lets us inspect that hierarchy without choosing one group count at the outset.

title: Density-Based Clustering
blurb: Groups need not form round clouds, and isolated observations need not belong to any group. We can instead ask where enough neighbours support extending a cluster.

title: Images as Arrays
blurb: Before a computer can find a seed in a photograph, it needs measurements to work with. We will look at the rows, columns, channels, and number types that make up an image.

title: Image Thresholding
blurb: A bright seed on a dark tray gives us a first rule to try. Compare each pixel with a cutoff, keep the result as a mask, and inspect where that rule fails.

title: Cleaning Masks With Morphology
blurb: A threshold can leave speckles and gaps. We can test a small shape against the mask to remove or connect particular structures, provided we understand what else that operation will change.

title: Connected Components
blurb: A mask tells us which pixels were selected. To count regions, we need a definition of connected and a way to give each reachable group its own label.

title: Image Augmentation
blurb: The same seed can appear in several positions or orientations. We can teach a model which changes should preserve an answer, but the transformation must keep the image and its labels consistent.

title: Transfer Learning
blurb: A model trained on other photographs may already measure useful visual patterns. We can test those features with a new prediction head before deciding whether the feature extractor also needs to change.

title: Bounding Boxes and Overlap
blurb: Knowing that a seed appears in a photograph does not tell us where it is. Rectangles give us a location to predict, and overlap gives us a way to compare that prediction with a labelled target.

title: Non-Maximum Suppression
blurb: A detector can report several rectangles around the same seed. We will rank candidates, keep a strong one, and remove sufficiently overlapping alternatives while preserving candidates for other objects.

title: What Would We Predict Before Fitting Anything?
blurb: Tomorrow's water demand is unknown. Yesterday's demand gives Botie a prediction he can actually make, and a reference that a more complicated forecast should improve on.

title: Building Inputs From Earlier Days
blurb: A prediction row needs information available before its target. We will turn one ordered record into rows of earlier readings without accidentally including the answer.

title: Separating Repetition From Change
blurb: A demand increase might be a lasting change or a normal part of the weekly schedule. Comparing like positions in a cycle helps us distinguish those possibilities.

title: Updating a Forecast Without Starting Over
blurb: Botie needs to respond to new demand without letting one unusual day replace everything he knows. A weighted update lets him control how quickly his estimate changes.

title: Learning From a Series' Own Past
blurb: A trailing average gives every lag the same influence. An autoregressive model fits different coefficients for the earlier readings and then uses that same rule to predict ahead.

title: Testing a Forecast as Time Moves Forward
blurb: One convenient cutoff can hide a forecasting failure. We will replay several prediction dates, preserving what was known at each one, and compare methods on matching targets.

title: Trying an Action Before Knowing Its Value
blurb: Botie can choose a watering schedule, but sees the result only for the schedule he actually tries. He must balance using his current favourite with learning about alternatives.

title: Describing What an Action Changes
blurb: Watering changes the greenhouse Botie will face tomorrow. A state, an action, and a transition model let us describe that consequence before choosing a policy.

title: Valuing Rewards That Arrive Later
blurb: An action can cost water now and help a plant later. A return combines a sequence of rewards so Botie can compare more than the immediate outcome.

title: Planning One Step, Then the Remaining Journey
blurb: A long sequence of choices is difficult to compare directly. We can combine the reward from one action with the value of the state it leaves behind, then improve those estimates repeatedly.

title: Learning Action Values From Experience
blurb: Botie may not know the transition probabilities. A sampled action, reward, and next state can still correct one entry in an action-value table.

title: Planning for More Than One Possible Outcome
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A delivery might contain different numbers of damaged sensors. Keep the possible outcomes and their probabilities together before deciding how many replacements to hold.

title: Updating an Unknown Failure Rate
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A few failed sensors give evidence about a failure rate, but do not determine it exactly. Keep a distribution over plausible rates and update it as results arrive.

title: Combining Measurements With Different Reliability
blurb: Two thermometers disagree. Their known error variances tell us how strongly each reading should influence a shared estimate.

title: Tracking a State We Cannot Observe Directly
blurb: An alarm does not directly reveal whether equipment is healthy. Combine how states change with how each state could produce the observed alarm.

title: Predicting Between Measurements With Uncertainty
blurb: Botie has measured temperature at only a few positions. A covariance rule connects nearby locations and describes how uncertain an unmeasured location remains.

title: Learning From a Few Records at a Time
blurb: Botie has more training records than he can process in one step. A batch gives him a manageable estimate of the direction in which to change the model.

title: Remembering the Direction of Earlier Updates
blurb: Successive batches can pull a weight in different directions. A stored velocity lets Botie carry some of the previous update direction into the next step.

title: Giving Different Weights Different Step Scales
blurb: Some parameters repeatedly receive larger gradients than others. Adam keeps separate running estimates of gradient direction and squared magnitude for each parameter.

title: Checking a Model Before a Long Training Run
blurb: A network can fail because its starting values suppress the signal or because its derivative is wrong. Test these separately before tuning the optimiser.

title: Deciding When a Training Run Has Done Enough
blurb: Training loss can improve after predictions on unseen records stop improving. Keep separate curves, choose a stopping rule in advance, and restore the best saved model.

title: Recommending Something Before Knowing the Reader
blurb: Botie has a shelf of guides and a record of which were opened. Begin with a popularity baseline, then examine what those records actually tell us.

title: Matching a Reader’s Interests to Guide Descriptions
blurb: Guide descriptions give us evidence even before a guide has been opened. Represent topics explicitly and compare them with a reader’s interests.

title: Learning From Readers With Similar Preferences
blurb: A guide’s description may miss what readers value. Shared ratings let Botie compare preferences, provided missing ratings remain distinct from dislikes.

title: Compressing a Sparse Table of Preferences
blurb: A rating table can be enormous and mostly empty. Small vectors for readers and guides can share information across its observed entries.

title: Checking the List a Reader Actually Sees
blurb: A recommender usually shows a short list. Evaluate that list’s relevant items, their positions, and the cases where little history is available.

title: Finding Unusual Readings Without Letting Them Set the Reference
blurb: A faulty sensor can pull an ordinary mean toward itself. Use a robust centre and spread, then decide what a large deviation actually warrants.

title: Judging a Reading Against Its Neighbours
blurb: Different operating regimes can have different spreads. Local outlier factor compares a point’s density with the density around its neighbours.

title: Finding Readings That Are Easy to Separate
blurb: An isolated reading often needs few random splits to stand apart. Follow paths through small trees before averaging that evidence across a forest.

title: Detecting Patterns a Model Cannot Reconstruct
blurb: A model trained to reproduce normal sensor patterns can expose departures through reconstruction error. The error still needs a validated alert rule.

title: Recording Which Things Are Connected
blurb: A table of pump readings leaves out the pipes between pumps. A graph records those relationships so calculations can use the connections.

title: Following Probability Through a Network
blurb: A random walker chooses among outgoing links. Follow the probability mass to see how graph structure changes where it accumulates.

title: Letting a Node Read Its Neighbours’ Measurements
blurb: A pump’s neighbours can provide useful context. Aggregate their readings while retaining the distinction between a node and its surroundings.

title: Learning From a Node and Its Neighbours Together
blurb: A graph convolution combines node features, self-connections, degree scaling, and learned weights. Work through these pieces before calling the result a layer.

title: Scoring Connections We Have Not Observed
blurb: Node representations can score possible links, but missing links are not guaranteed negatives. Design the split and candidate set before evaluating.

title: Separating a Useful Prediction From a Causal Claim
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Plants receiving extra water may grow poorly because they were already struggling. Compare the question a prediction answers with the question an intervention asks.

title: Making a Fair Comparison by Assignment
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Random assignment separates a treatment decision from the reasons a gardener might otherwise choose it. Estimate an average effect while keeping the experiment’s unit and uncertainty clear.

title: Comparing Treatments in the Same Population
blurb: When starting conditions affect treatment choice, standardisation can compare both treatments using one target population, if the measured conditions suffice to control confounding.

title: Reweighting Records Without Inventing Missing Evidence
blurb: Inverse-probability weighting changes which records count most. Understand the treatment probabilities and overlap assumptions before interpreting the resulting contrast.

title: Saving the Whole Prediction Procedure
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: Weights alone do not reproduce a prediction. Botie also needs feature order, fitted preparation, and the rules connecting them.

title: Checking What Arrives at the Model
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: A model can produce a number from the wrong columns or units. Define and validate the request before trusting its arithmetic.

title: Keeping a Prediction Consistent Across Requests
blurb: The same input should have the same preparation and result whether it arrives alone or in a batch. Keep prediction free of accidental fitting and mutable shared state.

title: Knowing Which Model Produced an Answer
blurb: A result needs a link to the model, preparation, data, and code that produced it. Version the prediction procedure so comparisons and rollbacks are meaningful.

title: Checking the Model After It Meets New Data
blurb: Inputs, outcomes, and service behaviour can change after launch. Monitor each separately and keep a tested route back to a known compatible version.

title: Investigate a Sensor Before Calling It Faulty
blurb: Fit a reference from earlier readings, select an alert rule on validation records, and evaluate that fixed rule on later labelled cases.

title: Forecast Tomorrow’s Water Demand Without Seeing Tomorrow
blurb: Build lagged inputs, compare an autoregressive model with persistence, and evaluate both through a sequence of later forecast origins.

title: Count Seeds While Keeping the Image Assumptions Visible
blurb: Turn a small tray image into a binary mask, label connected regions, and investigate when a region count stops matching the number of seeds.

title: What Would This Prediction Actually Change?
blurb: A model can flag a pump that may fail, but someone still has to decide what to do. Begin with that decision and work backwards to the information it needs.

title: Do We Need a Learned Model Yet?
blurb: A fixed rule already catches some faults. Work out what a learned model would have to improve before paying for its extra work.

title: What Can the System Know at Decision Time?
blurb: A reading can describe an earlier event and still arrive too late. Design a data contract that respects both clocks.

title: Where Does the Prediction Pipeline Run Out of Room?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: A fast model can sit inside a slow service. Follow requests through preparation, inference, and storage to find the stage that limits the whole path.

title: What Happens When Requests Arrive Together?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: Average demand can fit while a burst still leaves people waiting. Follow unfinished requests from one interval to the next.

title: Will the Model Fit on the Device?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: A model file can fit while its running process runs out of memory. Account for parameters, temporary values, and the rest of the runtime.

title: Should the Prediction Happen Here or on a Server?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: Sending an image away adds work before inference can begin. Compare communication and computation, then examine what happens when the connection disappears.

title: Which Designs Are Actually Acceptable?
blurb: A design can be fast, accurate, or inexpensive without meeting the job’s requirements. Remove infeasible options before comparing the choices that remain.

title: Which Assumption Could Change Our Decision?
blurb: An estimate can look convincing because its uncertain inputs were hidden. Vary the assumptions and find where the preferred design changes.

title: What Should the Prototype Teach Us?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: A prototype should answer a question that could change the design. Test interacting choices together instead of changing everything and guessing what helped.

title: What Should Happen When the Model Cannot Help?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: A missing reading or unavailable model still requires a response. Build a route that makes the failure visible and sends the case somewhere useful.

title: Can We Defend the Inspection Service Design?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: Bring the requirements back to the complete service. Check fault misses and queue capacity separately, then identify what the prototype still has not demonstrated.

title: What Makes This an Agent?
topic: From an Answer to an Action
blurb: Botie can describe a pump, but the technician needs its actual manual. Follow the software that lets a model ask for information and use what comes back.

title: How Do We Give an Agent a Job It Can Follow?
topic: Giving the Model a Clear Job
blurb: A technician wants help with a noisy pump. Begin prompt engineering with that job and its evidence, then test whether a clearer request produces a useful answer.

title: Can Another Program Use Botie’s Answer?
topic: Giving the Model a Clear Job
blurb: A technician can read a paragraph, but an application needs agreed fields. Check the response structure without confusing a valid record with a correct diagnosis.

title: When May Botie Turn a Suggestion into an Action?
blurb: Booking an inspection changes somebody’s work. Give the tool a precise interface, check the caller’s permission, and keep a retried request from creating a second job.

title: Which Records Should Botie Bring into the Conversation?
blurb: The manual collection is larger than one request can hold. Select permitted evidence, leave room for the reply, and keep each excerpt attached to its source.

title: What Should Botie Do After a Tool Replies?
blurb: One search may reveal that a second search is needed. Follow the observations through an agent loop, then give that loop explicit ways to finish or ask for help.

title: Does Botie Need to Choose the Next Step?
topic: Choosing How Much Autonomy to Give
blurb: A request to find a maintenance record and an investigation of an unfamiliar fault ask different things of the program. Compare what fixed steps can do before giving a model more decisions.

title: Give Botie a Typed Job with Pydantic AI
blurb: Botie can read a manual, but the application still needs a usable answer and real citation IDs. Give the agent its dependencies and check what comes back.

title: Put Limits Around a LangChain Agent
blurb: Botie keeps looking for a manual that does not exist. Use an agent runtime with explicit tool access and limits, then inspect the messages that explain its decisions.

title: Resume Botie’s Work with LangGraph
blurb: The technician returns after a pause. Preserve the right request’s evidence, merge updates deliberately, and resume a review without repeating an external action.

title: Ask Before Botie Creates the Inspection Job
blurb: A technician approves one inspection, then the proposal changes. Bind the decision to what was reviewed and check it again where the job is created.

title: Connect Botie to Tools with MCP
blurb: Several assistants need the same maintenance tools. Share an interface while keeping server identity, permissions and returned content visible.

title: What If the Manual Starts Giving Botie Orders?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: A retrieved maintenance note tells Botie to export records. Trace where that instruction came from, then keep the application’s permissions intact even when a screening model misses it.

title: Whose Pump Is Botie Allowed to Inspect?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: The tool name is allowed, but its arguments point at another customer’s asset. Build the service-side checks that connect the caller, operation and stored record.

title: How Much of the Maintenance Record Does Botie Need?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: A manual lookup needs an asset and a symptom, but the original record also contains private contact details. Build the smaller payload and control where it can go.

title: Can We Safely Use the Answer Botie Returned?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: A response can be valid JSON and still name the wrong pump or contain unwanted markup. Check its structure, its relationship to the request, and the context that will consume it.

title: Did Botie Create the Inspection, or Did the Reply Get Lost?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: A request times out after Botie submits an inspection. Work out what the service may already have done before sending another request.

title: Can Two of Botie’s Calls Spend the Same Remaining Budget?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: Two proposed lookups each appear affordable until they start together. Reserve shared resources before dispatch and keep the whole run within its operating limits.

title: Which Examples Should We Put in the Prompt?
blurb: Botie keeps making an inspection sound mandatory. Show what a supported answer looks like, then check that the examples teach the distinction we intended.

title: Why Did Botie Take So Long?
blurb: An answer arrives late, but the text cannot tell us where the time went. Follow one maintenance request through retrieval, tool calls and the final response.

title: Can We Find the Run Behind This Score?
blurb: A dashboard says answers improved. Connect scores to their requests and prompt versions so we can see which answers were actually checked.

title: What Would Count as Doing the Job?
blurb: A plausible answer can still come from an unacceptable sequence of actions. Build maintenance cases that check the answer, permitted tools and failure behaviour.

title: What Can We Test Without Calling a Model?
topic: Testing the Program Around the Model
blurb: An agent framework can run our tools, but a test model and a real model answer different questions. Build contract checks before spending time on live evaluations.

title: Who Checks the Model That Checks Botie?
blurb: Some answers need interpretation rather than an exact comparison. Give a judge a clear rubric, then test its judgements against evidence and human review.

title: Where Did the Answer First Go Wrong?
blurb: Several answers are wrong, but they did not fail for the same reason. Inspect the evidence and tool results before rewriting the prompt.

title: Did the New Examples Cause the Improvement?
blurb: A candidate improves after we change its model and prompt. Separate the changes, pair the task results, and inspect what became worse.

title: Is This Version Ready for the Next Shift?
blurb: A new agent can improve average answers while introducing an unacceptable failure. Compare the same cases and keep critical behaviour and operating budgets visible.

title: Can We Make Botie Cross the Boundary?
blurb: A guardrail passes our friendly examples. Try to break a specific boundary, inspect the actual effects, and check whether ordinary maintenance questions still work.

title: What Happens When the New Shift Finds a Failure?
blurb: The released assistant attempts an unapproved job. Stop further effects, account for work already in flight, and turn the failure into evidence for a careful restart.

title: Repair Botie’s Maintenance Assistant
topic: A Repair From Failure to Fresh Evidence
blurb: Follow a stale-manual failure through a test, a repair and a fresh evaluation. Keep unsupported answers and unapproved actions out of the release decision.

title: What Should Botie Be Unable to Do?
blurb: A helpful agent can still propose the wrong operation. Start with the effects we need to prevent, then put a control where each effect would happen.

title: Can Botie Fix the Bug Without Rewriting the Rules?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: The requested fix belongs in one function. The proposed patch also weakens its test. Review the actual changed files and keep verification outside the patch’s control.

title: Where Should Botie Run Code He Has Just Written?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: A test runner executes repository code. Give it a deliberately small environment, then verify the filesystem, network and resource limits that environment really enforces.

title: Are We Releasing the Code We Actually Checked?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: Botie adds a dependency and rebuilds the project. Bind the review and independent checks to the exact revision and artifact that will be released.

title: What Did We Actually Trust When We Connected the MCP Server?
blurb: A familiar tool name returns with a different description. Keep server identity, reviewed capabilities and individual calls separate as the connection changes.

title: A Valid Token for Which Service?
blurb: A token can be authentic and still belong to another API. Follow delegated authority from the caller to the MCP server without borrowing another service’s credentials.

title: What Exactly Did the Person Approve?
blurb: A reviewed action resumes after its target changes. Keep the approval, current object version and receiver’s action ledger together before allowing another write.

title: What Should Botie Pass to Another Agent?
blurb: A saved note and a delegated tool list can carry authority into a later run. Filter memory before use and restrict the child to the parent’s current grants.

title: Can the Repaired Agent Survive a Different Shift?
blurb: A refusal can arrive after an unauthorised tool call. Compare recorded effects with the intended policy, preserve blocked legitimate work and decide what evidence supports a limited release.
